newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-Polish finance minister change may boost Left.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Polish finance minister change may boost Left.

text.p: The replacement of controversial finance minister Grzegorz Kolodko signals little change in Poland's economic course, but may boost the ruling Left's chances in parliamentary polls this year, analysts said.
Kolodko, a non-party member whose resignation was accepted on Tuesday, was replaced by President Aleksander Kwasniewski's economic adviser Marek Belka.
Belka is seen as an independent economist with strong professional credentials but also as a man who is new to hardball politics.
He vowed to continue the policy of fiscal restraint to fight inflation, while speeding up key structural reforms.

Main opposition groups saw the move as an attempt by the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of ex-communists to boost their election chances by dumping their associate, the hot-tempered and unpopular Kolodko.

"This is a pre-election gesture...the coalition needed to find a scapegoat. Grzegorz Kolodko had not enjoyed great popularity and several of his decisions were not too wise," Piotr Zak, spokesman of the Solidarity trade union, told private Radio Zet.

"Kolodko is now defenceless, and can be used as a scapegoat for any accusations concerning the economy. During the election campaign he can be blamed," said Halina Franczak, an analyst at the independent Demoskop polling institute.
But a senior official of the SLD, the senior coalition partner, said Kolodko's resignation was his personal decision and he picked its timing.

"I think Professor Kolodko made the decision when the budget was approved. He decided that the passing of a good budget for 1997, which implements economic and social ideas he's been pursuing for three years, was a good moment to go," said Jerzy Szmajdzinski, head of the SLD parliamentary caucus.

Some analysts said the SLD might benefit from the move. But it was more a result of Kolodko's mounting conflict with ministers of the junior coalition partner, the Polish Peasant Party (PSL), than a premeditated SLD ploy.

"It seems that the resignation was more of a result of a personality conflict. The atmosphere in the government became so tense that something had to be done," said Bogdan Wyznikiewicz, a deputy head of the independent IBnGR economic think-tank.

"There are always politicians who become a target of all public frustrations and Kolodko has been such a figure in the last three years. Knowing Belka's style his appointment may help improve the public perception of the SLD," he added.

Kolodko, 47, has often clashed with other ministers and the rift became especially bitter last month when he openly criticised his cabinet colleagues for bowing to Peasant party demands to restore duties on feed grains.
Kolodko also blotted his copy book with voters last year by bitterly criticising those who legally took advantage of an expensive loophole his own ministry had left in tax rules.
"He has made the two unforgivable mistakes: He openly criticised his cabinet colleagues and...even worse, he criticised the electorate," Franczak told Reuters.
The SLD is now running neck-in-neck in opinion polls with a new powerful alliance of rightist parties grouped around Solidarity, with both winning support of 20-30 percent.
According to a survey by CBOS polling institute last month Grzegorz Kolodko and his Peasant party rival Agriculture Minister Roman Jagielinski have both plunged in popularity.
